full_text:
**Model family.** This is network science, specifically a dynamic or adaptive network under random (indiscriminate) rewiring. The node and edge counts are fixed. A random link is detached at one end and reattached to a uniformly random node. It is a null model for adaptive networks, and I treat it as a stochastic birth–death process on node degree.

**Expected behaviour, from my own derivation.**
- Each node gains a link at a constant rate of about 1/N.
- Each node loses a link at a rate proportional to its degree k, because it is more likely to sit at the end of the chosen link.
- Constant gain with linearly increasing loss gives a Poisson stationary degree distribution with mean equal to the mean degree. This is an Erdős–Rényi-like graph.
- The degree spread therefore stays at the Poisson value, with CV ≈ 1/√⟨k⟩. That is about 0.41 at mean degree 6 and 0.32 at mean degree 10. It does not grow into a heavy tail.
- Edges keep turning over, because a link is rewired at every step.
- I could not tell what the reported "n_degree_cv = -3.0" measures. It may be a z-score or a deviation from a baseline. Either way, a degree CV that stays at or below the random-graph value fits the Poisson result. A negative value would mean even less spread than the reference.

**What the literature says.**
- Arxiv 1001.3878, "Epidemic spreading in evolving networks", describes this exact scheme. One choice of rewiring yields an evolving ER-type network: choose a link at random and rewire one of its randomly chosen ends to a randomly chosen node. This scheme has a constant attachment rate and a linearly preferential detachment rate. It yields a Poisson degree distribution, and the rewired networks are uncorrelated.
- Gross, D'Lima and Blasius, "Epidemic Dynamics on an Adaptive Network", PRL 96, 208701 (2006), is the earliest clear source I verified. For state-independent rewiring, the degree distribution becomes Poissonian and the average degree of the next neighbours is independent of the degree.
- Arxiv 1606.05737, "Equilibrium distributions in entropy driven balanced processes", says networks resulting from unrestricted random rewiring should have their degree distribution in one of the Poisson, Bernoulli or Pólya classes.
- Gross and Blasius, "Adaptive coevolutionary networks: a review", J. R. Soc. Interface 5, 259–271 (2008), is the review. The search result confirms title, authors and venue. I did not read its section on random rewiring.
- The ALEA paper "Two evolving social network models" also states that its process reduces to random rewiring, so the degree distribution will be Poisson.

I did not trace the very earliest use of this scheme. It may predate the 2006 PRL paper.

**Verdict.** KNOWN. The model is a standard indiscriminate-rewiring null model for adaptive networks. The persistent edge turnover and the narrow, Poisson-like degree distribution are textbook results. The mean-degree-10 variant changes only the Poisson mean.

**Confidence.** High. The exact rule, a random link with one end moved to a uniform node, appears in a source I read. It is paired with the analytic Poisson result. The only uncertainty is how the "-3.0" metric is defined.
